newsitem.title: INDIA: FOCUS-India coalition inching towards raising oil prices.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-India coalition inching towards raising oil prices.

text.p: India's ruling coalition on Wednesday postponed a decision on whether to raise petroleum prices to plug a huge subsidy bill, but alliance officials said a price rise was inevitable and would come soon.

The United Front's decision-making Steering Committee, deeply divided over how to control a mounting bill for oil subsidies, met for 30 minutes but for the fourth time in three months deferred the decision.
"It has not been resolved," Information Minister Jaipal Reddy, who is coalition spokesman, told reporters after the meeting.
But a senior coalition official said the 15-party United Front could not put off the decision for much longer as the government owes oil companies billions of dollars.
"There is no option but to increase prices which we would do shortly," the official, who asked not to be identified, told reporters.

"We will meet very soon to take a final view on oil prices," Reddy said. "There was a feeling today that the decision on oil prices could not be put off for too long and we should meet very soon, though no date could be fixed."
"This time we are confident we will take a decision quickly."
The Press Trust of India (PTI) said the Steering Committee will meet again on August 21 to discuss the issue but there was no official confirmation of the meeting.
At the end of March, the government owed $4.3 billion to state oil firms, which sell some petroleum products such as kerosene to consumers at prices below world levels.
The government eventually reimburses the firms, but the bill -- called the oil pool deficit -- has kept rising because of the gap between Indian and international prices.
Communists in the 15-party coalition have strongly opposed proposals to raise the prices of some products, arguing that the move would hurt the poor.
But critics of the communists' plan, which would slash import duties on crude oil and raise taxes on luxury cars, say it would not curtail the cost of subsidies.
India's Congress party, which lends make-or-break parliamentary support to the United Front, last week said the oil pool deficit was threatening India's fiscal stability.
A crisis in Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's Janata Dal party, the biggest group in the 15-party coalition, was the main reason for the postponement of the earlier meetings.

The centre-left coalition jacked up petroleum prices shortly after assuming power in June 1996, saying the previous government led by the Congress party had failed to tackle the burgeoning oil subsidy bill.

Officials said that as part of a three-pronged plan to overhaul the oil sector, the government was also considering dismantling price controls and issuing bonds to state companies to delay repayment of the more than $4.3 billion in debt.
